water-cycle-s2.title: Where rain goes on two kinds of land

table.caption: What happens to 100 cm of yearly rain on a forested hillside and on a paved parking lot nearby (invented data for practice)

items.q: What supplies the energy that drives evaporation in the water cycle?
options: The sun
Earth’s gravity
The wind
Heat from inside the Earth

why.correct: Sunlight heats water and gives molecules the energy to escape as vapor. Gravity drives the downhill part: precipitation, runoff and infiltration.
options: Right: solar energy powers evaporation.
Gravity brings water down; it does not lift it.
Wind speeds evaporation but is itself driven by the sun.
Heat from inside the Earth is tiny compared with sunlight at the surface.

items.q: Which process moves water vapor from plants into the air?
options: Transpiration
Infiltration into soil
Condensation
Surface runoff

why.correct: Plants pull water up from roots and release vapor through small openings in their leaves.
options: Right: transpiration.
Infiltration is water soaking into the ground.
Condensation turns vapor into liquid droplets.
Runoff is water flowing over the surface.

items.q: Water vapor rises, cools and forms the droplets of a cloud. What is this step?
options: Condensation
Evaporation
Transpiration
Infiltration

why.correct: Cooling vapor turns back into tiny liquid droplets: condensation.
options: Right: vapor to liquid is condensation.
Evaporation is liquid to vapor.
Transpiration is vapor from plants.
Infiltration is water entering the soil.
Porous rock that holds groundwater
The area of land that drains into one river
A large lake formed behind a dam on a river
A low cloud that is full of water droplets

why.correct: An aquifer is porous rock or sediment that stores and transmits groundwater, which can be pumped from wells.
options: Right: an underground layer that holds and moves groundwater.
That describes the land that drains to one river, which is a different idea from an aquifer.
A lake behind a dam is a surface reservoir.
Clouds are in the air, not underground.

items.q: Why does heavy rain on dry, hard-packed soil often cause more runoff than the same rain on loose, moist soil?
options: Less water soaks in, so more flows off.
Hard soil makes more water evaporate during the storm.
Loose, moist soil repels the water that falls on it.
Dry soil pulls the storm clouds closer to the ground.

why.correct: When water cannot soak in fast enough, it flows over the surface as runoff.
options: Right: less infiltration means more runoff.
Evaporation during a storm is small and is not the reason.
Loose soil absorbs water.
Soil does not affect clouds.

items.q: Groundwater in some deep aquifers is thousands of years old. Why can pumping it faster than rain refills it be a problem?
options: It refills much more slowly than it is used.
Pumping the aquifer adds salt to the rain above it.
Groundwater turns into ice as soon as it is pumped up.
Pumping the aquifer makes nearby rivers flow uphill.

why.correct: Infiltration refills deep aquifers very slowly. Pumping faster than that lowers the water table, and wells must go deeper or run dry.
options: Right: withdrawal faster than recharge drains it.
Pumping does not add salt to rain.
Pumped groundwater stays liquid.
Rivers flow downhill whatever is pumped.

items.q: In a water cycle diagram, an arrow goes from the soil surface down to a layer of saturated rock. Which process is it?
options: Infiltration
Transpiration from leaves
Condensation
Precipitation from clouds

why.correct: Water soaking from the surface down into the ground is infiltration; it refills groundwater.
options: Right: water moving down into the ground.
Transpiration goes from plants to the air.
Condensation happens in the air.
Precipitation falls from clouds.

items.q: A town paves over a large meadow for a shopping center. Build the chain for what happens to the nearby creek during storms.

why.correct: Pavement stops infiltration, so more rain becomes runoff that reaches the creek quickly, raising flood peaks.

specific.frame: Pavement ___ infiltration, so ___ runoff reaches the creek quickly, and floods during storms become ___.

change.label: Effect on infiltration
options: reduces
increases

why.1: Pavement is hard and sealed, so water cannot soak in.

amount.label: Runoff
options: more
less

why.1: Water that cannot soak in flows over the surface, so runoff rises.

result.label: Floods
options: more likely
less likely

why.1: More water arriving faster raises the creek higher.

specific.model: Pavement reduces infiltration, so more runoff reaches the creek quickly during storms, which increases the water level and makes floods more likely.

items.q: About what share of Earth’s water is in the oceans?
options: About 96.5%
About 50.0%
About 3.5%
About 1.7%

why.correct: The ocean bar is at about 96.5%.
options: Right: almost all water is salty ocean water.
The ocean bar is far above half.
3.5% is roughly everything that is not ocean.
1.7% is the groundwater (or ice) bar.

items.q: Earth has about $1.39 \times 10^{9}$ cubic kilometers of water. Using the chart, about how many cubic kilometers are groundwater? Use 1.7%.

mistakes.why: You multiplied by 1.7, not by 1.7%. Divide the percent by 100 first: 1.7% = 0.017.
You divided by 1.7. A percent of a quantity is (percent / 100) × quantity.

items.q: Which conclusion about freshwater does the chart support?
options: Most freshwater is ice or groundwater.
Lakes and rivers hold most of the freshwater on Earth.
Freshwater makes up about half of the water on Earth.
Groundwater is the largest of the water reservoirs.

why.correct: Ice and groundwater are about 1.7% each, while lakes, rivers, soil and air together are well under 0.1%.
options: Right: ice and groundwater dwarf surface freshwater.
Lakes and rivers are in the smallest bar.
Freshwater is only a few percent of all water.
The oceans hold far more water than groundwater.

items.q: Why does the chart help explain why freshwater shortages happen even on a "water planet"?
options: Little water is fresh, liquid and easy to reach.
Most of the ocean is freshwater that people do not use.
Groundwater evaporates faster than ocean water does.
Ice caps melt and refill rivers in large amounts daily.

why.correct: About 96.5% is salty, and most freshwater is ice or deep groundwater, so easily reached freshwater is a tiny share.
options: Right: accessible freshwater is a tiny fraction.
Ocean water is salty.
Groundwater is underground and evaporates very little.
Melting ice feeds some rivers seasonally, not as a large daily supply.

items.q: How does paving change where rain goes, according to the table?
options: Runoff rises and infiltration falls.
Infiltration rises from 40 to 70 cm, and runoff falls.
Evaporation and transpiration double, from 25 to 50 cm.
Evaporation changes, but runoff and infiltration stay put.

why.correct: On the parking lot, runoff is 70 cm instead of 10, and infiltration is 5 instead of 40.
options: Right: much more runoff, much less infiltration.
The table shows the opposite.
They fall from 50 to 25 cm.
Runoff and infiltration change the most of the three paths.

items.q: What percent of the forest’s yearly rain infiltrates the ground?

mistakes.why: 0.4 is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for a percent: 40%.

items.q: Based on the table, what happens to the groundwater below a town as more land is paved?
options: It refills more slowly.
It is refilled faster, because the runoff soaks in.
It does not change, because the rain is the same.
It turns salty from chemicals on the pavement.

why.correct: Infiltration falls from 40 to 5 cm a year, so far less water reaches the groundwater.
options: Right: less infiltration means less recharge.
Runoff flows away over the surface rather than soaking in.
The same rain is split differently, so recharge changes.
Paving does not make groundwater salty by itself.

items.q: Cutting down most of the trees in a large rainforest region can reduce rainfall there. Why?
options: Less transpiration puts less vapor in the air.
Trees produce clouds from the surface of their bark.
Cutting trees makes the bare ground absorb more rain.
Trees pull rain in from the ocean through their roots.

why.correct: In rainforests much of the rain is water that the forest itself transpired. Remove the trees and that vapor supply drops.
options: Right: transpiration recycles water into the air.
Bark does not make clouds.
Cleared ground usually absorbs less, not more.
Roots draw water from the soil, not the ocean.
